title: Food banks
hook: ordinary church halls feeding neighbors every week

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jubilee 2000, and an old law where the field goes home. Your line was proclaim liberty. What did you let go of without mentioning it? Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Tuesday, four in the afternoon, a church hall that smells of floor polish and instant coffee. Folding tables in a row. Tins of beans, pasta, peanut butter, a crate of bread a bakery dropped off this morning. A retired teacher checks names on a list, kindly, without fuss. A teenager carries bags out to a car. A man in a work jacket studies the floor while he waits, until someone asks about his kids, and he looks up. None of this will reach a history book. Nobody will paint it. And next Tuesday the tables go up again. Today: food banks.

The words behind those tables are short. In Mark's Gospel a crowd has followed Jesus out to a lonely place, and it's getting late. The disciples suggest the sensible thing: send them away, so they can buy bread in the villages. Jesus answers, in the King James words: "Give ye them to eat." Not, leave it to me. You. The disciples protest that they can't afford it. He asks what they have. "Five, and two fishes." And the story ends with everyone fed and "twelve baskets full of the fragments" left over. Christians read that miracle in more than one way, but the order of the story is plain: the hungry are handed to the disciples, and what they already have is where it starts. Then Matthew 25, the passage that gave the hospice its line two days ago, a verse earlier. The king says to those on his right: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." They're puzzled. When? And he answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Read that way, the man in the work jacket is not a project. In the story's terms, Christ is standing in the line. That changes the posture: a chair, a name, a question about his kids. Not every food bank is run by a church, and churches don't all run them the same way. Some hand out bags. Some set up a small shop where people choose. Some cook a hot meal and sit down to eat with their guests. Some Christians press further and ask why the line is there at all: wages, rent, illness. Others say: feed today, argue tomorrow. Both are reading the same Gospels.
screen: `FIVE LOAVES: START WITH WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your cupboard in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture your kitchen shelves. What's there that you would be glad to eat yourself? Not the dented tin from the back. Something good. Choose one or two things. Then picture the hall: the folding table, the line, one face. If you pray, you can pray for whoever will open that bag. If you don't, just hold them in mind kindly. After the bell, set those things by the door, or look up the nearest food bank and what it needs this week. The bell holds the time.
Food banks. Church halls and other places where neighbors bring food and hand it to neighbors, week after week, behind them the command in Mark: give ye them to eat.
Your line: give them to eat. Today, set one good thing aside for a food bank, or buy one extra item at the store and drop it in the collection box. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 998 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CHURCH IN THE SOUTH.`

howItsDone: Church congregations host or support food banks and community meals, collecting food at services, staffing distribution days with volunteers, and pointing to Jesus's words in Mark 6 and Matthew 25.

match.prompt: the hall and the Gospels — tap the pairs.

sending them away was the disciples' idea. Jesus said: "give ye them to eat."

fork.setup: you're a disciple. it's late, the place is lonely, and a huge crowd is hungry. you have five loaves and two fish. what does Jesus tell you?
options: send them home to buy bread in the villages.
feed only the ones who came first.
fork.reveal: Mark 6:37. the disciples wanted to send the crowd away. Jesus handed the problem back to them, and started with what they had.

original.note: Greek: give ye them to eat (Mark 6:37). the Greek spells out the 'you' as well.

trapdoor: what you thought: a food bank is just charity.
what it means: in the Gospels, feeding the hungry is handed to the disciples, starting with what they have, and the hungry stranger is Christ himself.
what a scholar hears: Mark 6:37 sets an emphatic 'you' in the Greek, and Matthew 25:40 says the least of these are where Christ is met.

notes: The hook scene is an illustrative composite, not a report of a particular food bank.
Claims rule: no counts of food banks, guests or church involvement. 'Not every food bank is run by a church' and the three models (bags, small shops, hot meals) are general; confirm.
'Some Christians press further and ask why the line is there at all... Others say: feed today, argue tomorrow' presents two views without ranking; confirm fair.

The feeding story is paraphrased from Mark 6:34–44; the disciples' objection about cost (200 pennyworth) is summarized as 'they can't afford it'. 'Christians read that miracle in more than one way' is left general on purpose.
Original: Δότε αὐτοῖς ὑμεῖς φαγεῖν (Mark 6:37); confirm transliteration and the note that 'you' (ὑμεῖς) is explicit/emphatic.

Audit: Matthew 25 was also day 996's text (25:36); the teach now names that link so the reuse reads as deliberate. 'the story says... Christ is standing in the line' reframed as 'read that way... in the story's terms' so the narrator does not assert it.
